title: Fit Blocks Between Obstacles
statement:
There is a number line that starts at 0 and goes on to the right. Process queries in order. Each query is one of two kinds:

  • [1, x]: put an obstacle at position x. No obstacle is there yet.
  • [2, x, sz]: could a block of length sz be placed somewhere inside [0, x] without any obstacle strictly inside it? The block is not actually placed. It may touch obstacles with its ends, and it must lie completely within [0, x].

Return a list of booleans, one per query of kind 2, in order.

examples.why: With obstacles at 3 and 7, [0, 8] splits into free stretches of length 3, 4 and 1. A 4 fits between 3 and 7; a 5 fits nowhere.
Up to 4 the stretches are 2 and 2. Up to 5 the stretch after the last obstacle is 3 long. The piece between the last obstacle and x counts too.
An obstacle at 6 still lets a block of 6 touch it. Once 3 splits [0, 6] into 3 + 3, a 4 no longer fits.

constraints: No two kind-1 queries use the same x
hints: For a kind-2 query, the obstacles at or below x cut [0, x] into stretches, with 0 acting like an obstacle on the left end. The block fits if the longest stretch is at least sz. What are those stretches?

Store, at each obstacle position p, the length of the stretch that ends at p (p minus the previous obstacle). The answer is the max of those values over obstacles ≤ x, together with x minus the last obstacle ≤ x.

A segment tree over positions gives that prefix maximum in O(log X). Inserting an obstacle at x between neighbors p and q changes only two stored values: x − p at x, and q − x at q. Find p and q with binary search in a sorted list of obstacles.

explain.intuition:
Treat 0 as a permanent obstacle. The obstacles at or below x split [0, x] into consecutive stretches, and a block fits if and only if the longest stretch is at least sz. Two kinds of stretch matter: the ones between two consecutive obstacles, and the last one from the final obstacle up to x.

Attach each between-obstacles stretch to its right end: at obstacle q store q − prev(q). Then "longest closed stretch inside [0, x]" is a prefix maximum over positions ≤ the last obstacle before x, which a segment tree answers in O(log X). A new obstacle at x, between p and q, splits one stretch into two, so only two stored values change: position x gets x − p, and position q shrinks to q − x. Because values can shrink, a Fenwick tree for prefix maxima won't do here; a segment tree with point assignment will.
steps: Keep a sorted list of obstacles that starts as [0], and a max segment tree over positions 0..50 000, all zeros.
Kind 1 at x: find p (the obstacle just below x) and q (just above, if any) by binary search. Set tree[x] = x − p; if q exists set tree[q] = q − x. Insert x into the list.
Kind 2 at (x, sz): find p, the largest obstacle ≤ x. Let best = max(tree max over [0, p], x − p).
pitfalls: Forgetting the stretch from the last obstacle up to x, as in the second example.
Including stretches that end beyond x: an obstacle above x stores a length that reaches past the query's range.
Updating only the new obstacle's value and not shrinking the next obstacle's value, which keeps reporting the old, longer stretch.

complexity.time: O(q log X), plus O(q) per insertion into the array-backed sorted list (fast memmove in practice)

solutions.title: Scan the sorted obstacles
solutions.idea: Keep the obstacles sorted. For each kind-2 query, walk the obstacles up to x and measure every stretch.

solutions.title: Segment tree of stretch lengths
solutions.idea: Store each closed stretch's length at its right obstacle in a max segment tree. A query is a prefix max plus the open stretch up to x; an insertion changes two values.

followups: Solve it offline: place all obstacles first and process the queries backwards, so obstacles are only removed. Why does a Fenwick tree of prefix maxima now work?
Return the leftmost position where the block fits instead of a yes/no. How do you descend the segment tree to find it?
